The result moves around from one threshold to the next, partly because the number of patients falls as the threshold rises; a single threshold should not be read too precisely. ## How different the two breasts are ::: {#cell-fig-differences .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} def signed_differences(min_height, min_centre, rejected=False): """{comparison: [first-named − second Water:Fat per patient]}, and {"NORMAL vs NORMAL": [left − right]}.""" found = rule_breasts(min_height, min_centre, rejected=rejected) out = defaultdict(list) for nova in sorted({n for n, _ in found if (n, "LEFT") in found and (n, "RIGHT") in found}): (label_a, ratio_a, *_), (label_b, ratio_b, *_) = found[nova, "LEFT"], found[nova, "RIGHT"] if not (np.isfinite(ratio_a) and np.isfinite(ratio_b)): continue for comparison, (base, others) in COMPARISONS.items(): if label_a == base and label_b in others: out[comparison].append(ratio_b - ratio_a) elif label_b == base and label_a in others: out[comparison].append(ratio_a - ratio_b) if label_a == label_b == "NORMAL": out["NORMAL vs NORMAL"].append(ratio_a - ratio_b) return out signed_rule = signed_differences(WATER_MIN, CENTRE_MIN) signed_rejected = signed_differences(WATER_MIN, CENTRE_MIN, rejected=True) rng = np.random.default_rng(1) plt.rcParams["font.size"] = 7 # small text so both panels fit side by side on an A4 page fig, (signed_ax, size_ax) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 4.2)) for ax in (signed_ax, size_ax): ax.set_box_aspect(1) # square panels names_signed = list(COMPARISONS) + ["NORMAL vs NORMAL"] # NN is LEFT − RIGHT names_size = list(COMPARISONS) + ["NORMAL vs NORMAL"] for ax, names_here, transform in ((signed_ax, names_signed, lambda v: v), (size_ax, names_size, lambda v: [abs(x) for x in v])): groups = [] for k, name in enumerate(names_here): groups.append((k - 0.2, transform(signed_rule.get(name, [])), USABLE_COLOUR)) groups.append((k + 0.2, transform(signed_rejected.get(name, [])), REJECTED_COLOUR)) box_with_points(ax, groups, rng) ax.set_xticks(range(len(names_here))) ax.set_xticklabels([f"{n.replace(' vs ', chr(10) + 'vs ')}\n(n = {len(signed_rule.get(n, []))} / {len(signed_rejected.get(n, []))})" for n in names_here], fontsize=6) ax.grid(alpha=0.3, axis="y") signed_ax.axhline(0, color="black", lw=1) signed_ax.set(ylabel="first-named − second, Water:Fat", title="Which breast has more water") size_ax.set(ylabel="|A − B|, Water:Fat", title="How different the two breasts are", ylim=(0, None)) from matplotlib.patches import Patch signed_ax.legend(handles=[Patch(color=USABLE_COLOUR, alpha=0.5, label="usable scans"), Patch(color=REJECTED_COLOUR, alpha=0.5, label="rejected scans")], frameon=False, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(1.1, -0.2), ncols=2, fontsize=6) fig.tight_layout() plt.show() plt.rcParams["font.size"] = 10 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Each patient's two breasts compared, using only the usable scans (blue) or only the rejected scans (grey); one dot per patient. **Left**: the signed difference, first-named − second (CANCER − NORMAL, etc.; NORMAL vs NORMAL is LEFT − RIGHT); above 0, the first-named breast has more water. **Right**: |A − B|, which does not need to know which breast is which. Boxes span the middle half of the patients, the thick line is the median, and the whiskers reach the furthest patient within 1.5 box-lengths.](glandular_details_files/figure-html/fig-differences-output-1.png){#fig-differences width=768 height=386} ::: ::: The rule accepts 39% of all scans. The results using **only the usable scans**: | Usable scans | First-named breast higher | Median difference between the breasts, \|A − B\| | |---|---|---| | CANCER vs NORMAL | **15/18 \(83%\)** | 1\.00 | | BENIGN vs NORMAL | **10/27 \(37%\)** | 0\.66 | | CANCER vs BENIGN | **2/5 \(40%\)** | 2\.22 | | **NORMAL vs NORMAL** | – | **0\.58** (2 patients) | and the same comparisons using **only the scans the rule rejects**, the other 61% (each breast is the mean of its rejected scans, and a patient is compared only if both breasts have one): | Rejected scans | First-named breast higher | Median difference between the breasts, \|A − B\| | |---|---|---| | CANCER vs NORMAL | **11/23 \(48%\)** | 0\.13 | | BENIGN vs NORMAL | **16/31 \(52%\)** | 0\.12 | | CANCER vs BENIGN | **14/20 \(70%\)** | 0\.16 | | **NORMAL vs NORMAL** | – | **0\.08** (9 patients) | The **difference between the breasts** is |A − B| of the two breasts' Water:Fat, the median over the patients in each row. Because every curve is already normalised so its fat peak is 1, the absolute gap has a direct meaning and needs no further scaling. It does not need to know which breast is which, so it is what a blind measurement would see. **NORMAL vs NORMAL** is the baseline: how different two healthy breasts of the same patient are. If a cancer is to be spotted blind, a CANCER/NORMAL pair has to differ by clearly more than that. From the usable scans, the CANCER breast is the higher in **15/18 \(83%\)** of CANCER/NORMAL patients, and the two breasts differ by a median of **1\.00**. From the rejected, fatty scans it is the higher in only **11/23 \(48%\)**, about what chance would give, and the breasts differ by **0\.13**, close to the **0\.08** of two NORMAL breasts. Fatty scans cannot tell a CANCER breast from a NORMAL one; the information is in the water-rich scans. The NORMAL vs NORMAL baseline is thin, though: 2 patients have two NORMAL breasts with usable scans and 9 with rejected scans. ## Usable and rejected scans by age {#sec-usable-and-rejected-scans-by-age} Breasts are averaged within each age band, separately for NORMAL, BENIGN and CANCER, twice: once using only the scans that pass the test (usable), and once using only the scans it rejects. In each, a breast is the mean of the scans used. This shows what the kept and the discarded scans look like at different ages. ::: {#cell-fig-usable-by-age .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} plot_bands(summaries["usable"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![**Usable scans.** Mean prepared curve of NORMAL, BENIGN and CANCER breasts, one panel per age band (each breast is the mean of its usable scans), with ±1 SD across breasts shaded. One point per breast; a least-squares line and Spearman ρ per label. ::: {#cell-fig-usable-normal .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} import h5py from scipy.stats import spearmanr # age is stored per scan in the HDF5; one value per Nova _nova_age = {} with h5py.File(ne.STORE_PATH, "r") as _store: for _group in _store["scans"].values(): _nova = int(_group.attrs["nova"]) _age = float(_group.attrs.get("age", np.nan)) if np.isfinite(_age): _nova_age[_nova] = _age def _age_water_points(label): ages, waters = [], [] for (nova, side, lab), curves in breast_use.items(): if lab != label or nova not in _nova_age: continue with warnings.catch_warnings(): warnings.simplefilter("ignore", RuntimeWarning) mean_curve = np.nanmean(curves, axis=0) water_h = float(np.nanmean(mean_curve[(q >= WATER[0]) & (q <= WATER[1])])) if not np.isfinite(water_h): continue ages.append(_nova_age[nova]) waters.append(water_h) return np.asarray(ages, float), np.asarray(waters, float) _age_water_by_label = {lab: _age_water_points(lab) for lab in COHORTS} _age_water_stats = {lab: spearmanr(ages, waters) for lab, (ages, waters) in _age_water_by_label.items() if len(ages) >= 2} plt.rcParams["font.size"] = 7 fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.8, 3.8)) ax.set_box_aspect(1) for label in COHORTS: ages, waters = _age_water_by_label[label] if len(ages) < 2: continue rho, p_val = _age_water_stats[label] colour = ne.STATUS_COLOURS[label] ax.scatter(ages, waters, s=18, color=colour, alpha=0.75, lw=0, zorder=3, label=f"{label} (n = {len(ages)}, ρ = {rho:.2f})") fit = np.polyfit(ages, waters, 1) line_x = np.linspace(ages.min(), ages.max(), 50) ax.plot(line_x, np.polyval(fit, line_x), color=colour, lw=1.4, zorder=2) ax.axhline(WATER_MIN, color="black", lw=1, alpha=0.45, ls="--") ax.set(title="Usable breasts: water peak vs age", xlabel="Age (years)", ylabel="Water peak height (q 20–22)") ax.grid(alpha=0.3) ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper right", fontsize=6) fig.tight_layout() plt.show() plt.rcParams["font.size"] = 10 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![All usable breasts: water peak height (mean over q 20–22 of the breast's usable-scan mean) against patient age. Points coloured by label; solid line is ordinary least squares within that label; dashed line is the usable-scan water threshold.](glandular_details_files/figure-html/fig-usable-normal-output-1.png){#fig-usable-normal width=354 height=365} ::: ::: In every usable cohort the link runs the same way — **older → lower water peak (fattier)** — Spearman ρ = \-0\.39 NORMAL (p = 0\.0017), \-0\.28 BENIGN (p = 0\.0015), \-0\.43 CANCER (p = 0\.0066). ## Who the rule leaves out Who are the patients the rule cannot compare? Of the 187 patients with both breasts scanned (NORMAL, BENIGN or CANCER), the rule compares **85** and leaves out **102**: 37 with one breast without a usable scan and 65 with neither. The pathology and radiology sheets in `Images/` were searched for each patient, independently of the scattering data. ::: {#cell-fig-who-left-out .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} plt.rcParams["font.size"] = 7 fig, (density_ax, age_ax) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 4.6)) for ax in (density_ax, age_ax): ax.set_box_aspect(1) width = 0.38 for offset, group, colour in ((-width / 2, "compared", USABLE_COLOUR), (width / 2, "left out", REJECTED_COLOUR)): shares = [100 * density_share[group][c] for c in DENSITY_ORDER] density_ax.bar(np.arange(len(DENSITY_ORDER)) + offset, shares, width=width, color=colour, alpha=0.75, label=f"{group} ({len(rule_groups[group])} patients)") for k, s in enumerate(shares): density_ax.text(k + offset, s + 1, f"{s:.0f}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=5.5) density_ax.set_xticks(range(len(DENSITY_ORDER))) density_ax.set_xticklabels(DENSITY_ORDER, fontsize=5.5, rotation=35, ha="right", rotation_mode="anchor") density_ax.set(ylabel="patients (%)", title="Breast density in the radiology reports", ylim=(0, 80)) density_ax.grid(alpha=0.3, axis="y") density_ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=6, loc="upper left") box_with_points(age_ax, [(0, group_ages["compared"], USABLE_COLOUR), (1, group_ages["left out"], REJECTED_COLOUR)], np.random.default_rng(2)) age_ax.set_xticks([0, 1]) age_ax.set_xticklabels([f"compared\n(n = {len(group_ages['compared'])})", f"left out\n(n = {len(group_ages['left out'])})"]) age_ax.set(ylabel="age (years)", title=f"Age (Mann-Whitney p = {age_p:.1g})") age_ax.grid(alpha=0.3, axis="y") fig.tight_layout() plt.show() plt.rcParams["font.size"] = 10 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Patients the rule compares (blue) and leaves out (grey). **Left**: BI-RADS breast density, the category the radiology reports mention most often for each patient. **Right**: age, where the sheets give it; one dot per patient.](glandular_details_files/figure-html/fig-who-left-out-output-1.png){#fig-who-left-out width=765 height=439} ::: ::: The pattern is clear (@fig-who-left-out): **the rule leaves out the fatty breasts.** Radiologists describe a mostly fatty breast as having “scattered areas of fibroglandular density” (BI-RADS B); that is the main description for **52%** of the patients left out but only **8%** of those compared. The patients compared are mostly heterogeneously or extremely dense (BI-RADS C/D: 82%, against 39% of those left out). They are also younger, median **45** against **59** years, as expected since breasts become fattier with age. | Mentioned in the patient's records | Compared | Left out | p (Fisher) | |---|---|---|---| | “scattered areas of fibroglandular density” \(mostly fatty\) | 8% | 54% | 1e\-11 | | “dense” \(any\) | 85% | 49% | 3e\-07 | | “extremely dense” | 18% | 3% | 0\.0008 | | “palpable” | 41% | 22% | 0\.004 | | “screening \(asymptomatic\)” | 25% | 38% | 0\.06 | | “calcification” | 76% | 89% | 0\.03 | | “carcinoma” | 29% | 40% | 0\.2 | | “mastitis” | 8% | 2% | 0\.08 | | “family history” | 4% | 2% | 0\.7 | Patients who came in with a palpable lump, often younger women with dense breasts, are more often compared; routine screening patients lean towards being left out. Mastitis and family history make no clear difference. ::: {.callout-note title="What this means"} 1. **The rule is, in effect, a breast-density filter.** Its scan-by-scan water-peak check, which never sees the clinical records, keeps mostly BI-RADS C/D breasts and drops mostly B. This confirms from independent records that rejected scans come from fatty tissue, not from bad measurements. 2. **This is where it would be most useful.** Dense breasts are where mammography is weakest (the reports here repeatedly say density “may obscure small masses”), so a method that works in dense breasts would complement it. 3. **It narrows who the result applies to.** The CANCER vs NORMAL result of the rule holds for younger women with dense breasts; for the older, fattier group it currently says nothing. 4. **Age cannot bias the comparison itself**: both breasts of a patient have the same age, so age decides only *who* is compared, not which breast comes out higher. ::: ### Is it just the odds of hitting glandular tissue? A dense breast holds more glandular tissue, so a scan placed anywhere in it is more likely to pass through some. The table shows, for each density, how often a scan is usable, how often a patient ends up with both breasts usable, and how often a breast's scans disagree (some usable, some rejected): | Density | Patients | Scans usable | Patients with both breasts usable | Breasts whose scans disagree | |---|---|---|---|---| | A: almost entirely fatty | 4 | 0% | 0% | 0% | | B: scattered fibroglandular | 60 | 11% | 12% | 16% | | C: heterogeneously dense | 94 | 49% | 60% | 40% | | D: extremely dense | 16 | 82% | 88% | 16% | | not stated | 13 | 53% | 62% | 31% | **Density sets the odds.** A single scan is usable in 11% of cases in mostly fatty (B) breasts and 82% in extremely dense (D) ones. That is why the rule leaves out the fatty breasts. **A breast's scans usually agree.** Most breasts give all usable or all rejected scans. If each scan were an independent coin flip, about 71% of C breasts would have a mix; only 40% do. The scans are taken close together and sample the same region, so if a scan misses, moving to a clearly different spot should help more than repeating nearby. **Age matters even at the same density:** | Density | Chance a scan is usable, age < 50 | age ≥ 50 | |---|---|---| | B: scattered fibroglandular | 29% (7 patients) | 7% (24 patients) | | C: heterogeneously dense | 58% (28 patients) | 29% (19 patients) | Within the same BI-RADS category, younger patients' scans are usable two to four times as often. Either BI-RADS, a coarse four-step scale, hides real differences in density, or glandular tissue itself holds less water with age (it involutes after menopause, with fewer cells and more collagen), so even a scan that does hit it may not show a water peak above the threshold. This data cannot separate the two, and the groups are small.
